'''Hyatt M. Gibbs''' (6 August 1938 – 3 September 2012) was a notable physicist and professor at the [[University of Arizona College of Optical Sciences]].<ref name="lqp">{{cite web
 |last=Waller 
 |first=Kristin 
 |title=In Memoriam: Hyatt M. Gibbs 
 |website=lqp.arizona.edu
 |date=12 September 2012 
 |url=http://lqp.arizona.edu/node/6827
 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20121210072309/http://lqp.arizona.edu/node/6827
 |url-status=dead
 |archive-date=10 December 2012
 |accessdate=17 September 2012 
}}</ref>  Well known for research in [[nonlinear optics]] and [[quantum optics]], he authored a book on [[optical bistability]], and was a recipient of the [[Humboldt Prize|Humboldt Research Award]] and Michelson Medal.<ref name="resume">{{cite web|title=Hyatt M. Gibbs |publisher=[[University of Arizona College of Optical Sciences]] |date=August 2009 |url=http://www.optics.arizona.edu/Faculty/Resumes/Gibbs.htm |accessdate=17 September 2012 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://archive.today/20120814053004/http://www.optics.arizona.edu/Faculty/Resumes/Gibbs.htm |archivedate=August 14, 2012 }}</ref><ref name="book">{{Citation
 | last = Gibbs
 | first = Hyatt
 | title = Optical Bistability: Controlling Light With Light
 | place = Orlando, Florida
 | publisher = Academic Press
 | year = 1985
 | isbn = 0122819403}}</ref>

==Education==
Gibbs attended [[Mars Hill College]] and [[North Carolina State University]] in his home state, where he earned an A.A. degree in 1958 and a B.S. degree in 1960, respectively.<ref name="resume" />  In 1965, he earned a Ph.D. in physics from the [[University of California at Berkeley]] with his thesis on ''Total Spin-Exchange Cross-Sections for Alkali Atoms from Optical Pumping Experiments''.<ref>
{{Citation
 | last = Gibbs
 | first = Hyatt
 | title = Total Spin-Exchange Cross-Sections for Alkali Atoms from Optical Pumping Experiments
 | publisher = [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]], [[University of California at Berkeley]]
 | date = 12 March 1965
 | bibcode = 1965PhDT........33G
 | osti = 4595958
 }}</ref>

==Career==
After earning his Ph.D., Gibbs remained at U.C. Berkeley as an Acting Assistant Professor until 1967.  He then joined [[Bell Labs]] in Berkeley Heights, New Jersey where he worked until 1980.<ref name="resume" />  During his work there he collaborated on numerous experiments, including research on optical energy transfer in crystals with Samuel L. McCall and [[Steven Chu]], a [[Nobel Prize]] winner and the [[United States Secretary of Energy]].<ref>{{cite journal
 | last = Chu
 | first = Steven
 | authorlink = Steven Chu
 | title = The Manipulation of Neutral Particles
 | journal = Nobel Lectures, Physics 1996-2000
 | pages = 122
 | publisher = World Scientific Publishing Co.
 | location = Singapore
 | date = January 2003
 | url = https://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/physics/laureates/1997/chu-lecture.pdf
 | isbn = 981-238-003-5
 | accessdate = 17 September 2012}}</ref>  For one year during this period, 1975 to 1976, he was an exchange scientist at [[Philips]] in Eindhoven, Holland.  He was also a visiting lecturer at [[Princeton University]] from 1978 to 1979.<ref name="resume" />

In 1980 he moved to Tucson, Arizona to become a professor at the [[University of Arizona College of Optical Sciences|Optical Sciences Center]] at the [[University of Arizona]].  Here he founded the ''Optical Circuitry Cooperative'' in 1984, which conducted research relevant to [[optical computing|optical processing]], funded jointly by industry leaders in [[optics]] and [[optoelectronics]].<ref name="resume" />  He remained its director until 1991 when the role was given to his collaborator, Dr. Nasser Peyghambarian.<ref>{{cite web
 |title       = Nasser Peyghambarian
 |publisher   = [[University of Arizona College of Optical Sciences]]
 |url         = http://optsc-cianerc.catnet.arizona.edu/contacts/nasser_profile.cfm
 |accessdate  = 17 September 2012
 |url-status     = dead
 |archiveurl  = https://web.archive.org/web/20130117024719/http://optsc-cianerc.catnet.arizona.edu/contacts/nasser_profile.cfm
 |archivedate = 17 January 2013
}}</ref>  Gibbs was able to concentrate more fully on his research, particularly his work with Dr. [[Galina Khitrova]] (whom he married in 1986) and [[Stephan W. Koch|Dr. Stephan W. Koch]] on the quantum nano-optics of semiconductors.<ref name="qnos">{{cite web
 | title = QNOS: Quantum Nano-Optics of Semiconductors
 | publisher = [[University of Arizona College of Optical Sciences]]
 | url = http://www.optics.arizona.edu/qnos/
 | accessdate = 17 September 2012}}</ref>  Gibbs became a professor emeritus in 2011, but continued his work until his death in 2012.<ref name="lqp" />

== Asteroid Hyatt ==
The unusual main-belt asteroid [[221628 Hyatt]] was named in his honor on 3 July 2012 ({{small|[[Minor Planet Circulars|M.P.C.]] 79912}}),<ref name="MPC-Circulars-Archive">{{cite web |title = MPC/MPO/MPS Archive |work = Minor Planet Center |url = https://www.minorplanetcenter.net/iau/ECS/MPCArchive/2012/MPC_20120703.pdf |accessdate = 14 April 2018}}</ref> just two months before he died. The asteroid was discovered by his son [[Alex R. Gibbs|Alex Gibbs]] of the [[Catalina Sky Survey]], who proposed the name to the [[Minor Planet Center]] of the [[International Astronomical Union]].<ref>{{cite web
 |title = (221628) Hyatt |publisher = Minor Planet Center |url = http://www.minorplanetcenter.net/db_search/show_object?object_id=hyatt |accessdate = 17 September 2012}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Gibbs' first marriage was to Lethia, with whom he had a son, Alex, and a daughter, Vanetta.  His second marriage was to Galina Khitrova, with whom he collaborated professionally.<ref name="qnos" />  On September 3, 2012, Hyatt M. Gibbs died in France at the age of 74 from mesothelioma complications.<ref name="lqp" />
